limited.t: Every patient is reviewed at multidisciplinary conference before listing, before bridging or downstaging starts, and at each restaging interval.
limited.why: Guideline consensus, extended locally. NCCN supports multidisciplinary transplant-center assessment; reviewing before every treatment start and at each restaging (about 3-monthly while waiting) is the protocol's own frequency, and it cites no study of how often review is needed or what it changes. Track the interval from restaging to conference decision and how often review changes the plan.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2 Multidisciplinary Team (restaging interval in §4.3 Restaging While on Waitlist)

limited.t: After successful downstaging no institutional stability period is added; timing follows the allocation rules (imaging ≥4 weeks after the last treatment and the 6-month wait from the first exception request).
limited.why: Local choice resting on allocation rules, not outcome data. The 2012 international consensus noted that at least 3 months of observation after downstaging was often recommended, but that was never a randomized optimization of observation time; waiting longer may expose aggressive biology but also adds dropout and decompensation risk. Track recurrence and dropout by time from successful downstaging to transplant.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §7.4 Observation Period

limited.t: Before elective LDLT an observation interval with sustained tumor control is documented; a proposed 3-month local default applies and any departure needs explicit MDT rationale.
limited.why: Consensus-informed local default. The protocol labels 3 months a conservative proposal, not a validated threshold. Its source, the 2012 international consensus, describes considering an observation period such as 3 months to judge tumor behavior but does not make it mandatory, and no comparison of intervals is cited; longer observation can also add dropout risk. Track recurrence and pre-transplant dropout by observation interval among LDLT recipients.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §8 Living Donor Liver Transplantation (LDLT)

limited.t: Bevacizumab is stopped at least 28 days before elective surgery and not restarted for at least 28 days after major surgery and wound healing; transplant timing may need a longer individual interval.
limited.why: Extrapolated from the drug label. The 28-day minimum comes from the US prescribing information for elective surgery; the protocol states it is not a proven safe interval for liver transplantation and cites no transplant-specific study. Track wound, bleeding and vascular complications in recipients with recent anti-VEGF exposure.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §6 Bridging and treatment-to-transplant interface (Systemic exposure and operative safety); same text in high-risk pathway document §4.1

limited.t: After transplant: contrast abdominal CT/MRI and chest CT every 3–6 months for 2 years, then 6-monthly to year 5, with AFP; the explant RETREAT score guides surveillance intensity.
limited.why: Extrapolated from a general HCC schedule and a prognostic score. The schedule follows NCCN post-treatment follow-up, which the protocol notes is not proof of an optimal transplant-specific or RETREAT-specific schedule; its review sources call risk-adapted surveillance promising but without prospective proof of the best frequency or duration. Track stage at detection of recurrence, salvage treatment and survival by RETREAT stratum.

limited.t: mTOR-containing CNI minimization may be considered individually for renal or oncologic-risk reasons (everolimus not before day 30); it is not offered as proven prevention of recurrence.
limited.why: Conditional (weak, level 3) guideline suggestion; the randomized trial missed its primary endpoint. In SiLVER (525 randomized recipients) recurrence-free survival did not differ significantly; benefit appeared only over the first 3–5 years and in exploratory, unpowered subgroups. The AASLD/AST suggestion is confined to HCC within Milan. Track recurrence, renal function and mTOR toxicity by regimen.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §10.2 mTOR Inhibitor Consideration

limited.t: For recurrence after transplant, multikinase inhibitors (sorafenib, lenvatinib) are the usual first systemic choice; checkpoint inhibitors are exceptional salvage after transplant-oncology review.
limited.why: Local convention. The protocol cites no source or comparative post-transplant trial for the first-choice statement. Avoiding checkpoint inhibitors rests on one retrospective series of 52 recipients (32 with HCC) in which seven had rejection and five died of it; pre-transplant safety estimates do not transfer to this setting. Track response, rejection, graft loss and survival for every systemic regimen used after transplant.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §11.3 Management of Recurrence

limited.t: For selected oligorecurrence after transplant, complete resection is considered; intrahepatic recurrence is treated with ablation, radiation or intra-arterial therapy chosen case by case.
limited.why: Selected retrospective series. The protocol states that the observational survival advantage of resection is strongly selection-confounded and that the local modalities are not supported as equivalent by transplant-specific comparative trials; part of the radiation evidence comes from non-transplant cohorts. Track morbidity, graft function and survival after each salvage treatment.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §11.3 Management of Recurrence

limited.t: Program audit targets: five-year post-transplant overall survival above 70% and five-year cumulative HCC recurrence below 15%, both provisional and pending committee approval.
limited.why: Local benchmarks, not validated thresholds. The cited systematic review describes five-year survival above 70% in selected Milan cohorts with recurrence commonly 10–20%, but calculates no pooled estimate or quality trigger, and its reported recurrence range is not consistently below 15%. A result outside target prompts case-mix and process review, not an automatic finding of preventable failure.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §13 Quality Metrics and Outcomes Tracking

limited.t: After prior checkpoint-inhibitor exposure the standard institutional regimen is used: ATG, tacrolimus 12–15 ng/mL, rapid steroid withdrawal and protocol biopsies are not mandated; rejection watch continues past month 1.
limited.why: Absence of evidence. The intensified options are author proposals from small heterogeneous reports, and no immune assay, ATG regimen or high tacrolimus target is validated. Prior immune toxicity marks higher rejection risk in retrospective cohorts but does not show that intensification prevents it, and rejection has occurred after the first month. Track biopsy-proven rejection, its timing, graft loss and infection by prior-ICI and immune-toxicity status.

summary.text: Single-arm: 174/209 (83.3%) down-staged; 2-y dropout 37.3%; 46.6% transplanted by 3 y; 2-y post-LT survival 95%; 42.8% of explants beyond Milan

appraisal.note: Prospective multicenter UNOS-downstaging cohort. The current allocation policy controls exact numerical boundaries; cohort selection does not establish exception approval.
appraisal.scope: Prospective MERITS-LT cohort: 209 UNOS-DS patients at seven centers in four US regions, 2016–2019.
appraisal.results: 174/209 (83.3%) achieved downstaging; two-year estimated success 87.7%. Observed dropout was 75/209, including 51 tumor progressions and nine liver-related deaths; two-year competing-risk dropout 37.3%. LT occurred in 63/209 by cutoff; three-year LT probability 46.6%. Median post-LT follow-up 1.7 years; two-year recipient survival 95%, three-year 83.1%; recurrence 5/63. Three-year treatment-entry survival 73%. Explants exceeded Milan in 42.8%, with microvascular invasion in 17.5%.
appraisal.limitations: Early post-LT follow-up and substantial radiology/explant discordance; success of an imaging endpoint does not establish absence of viable cancer. Overlaps later MERITS expansions.

summary.lead: Prospective nine-centre cohort · 190 all-comers vs 326 UNOS-DS
summary.text: All-comers vs UNOS-DS: two-year downstaging 66% vs 82%; five-year ITT survival 45.0% vs 58.8%; post-LT recurrence 29.8% vs 13.7%

appraisal.scope: National prospective cohort, nine centers, 2015–2023: 190 all-comers and 326 UNOS-DS patients; intention-to-treat clock starts at first locoregional treatment.
appraisal.results: Two-year downstaging: 66% versus 82%. Among all-comers, number plus largest diameter <10, 10–12 and >12 had success of 72%, 51% and 39%. Five-year treatment-entry survival: 45.0% versus 58.8%. LT occurred in 76/190 versus 155/326; median downstaging-to-LT 10.6 months. The exclusions cite the AASLD/AST candidate-evaluation guideline, whose prior-treatment background list the protocol warns must not be stretched to protocol-directed neoadjuvant therapy. No outcome data for previously resected or pretreated candidates are cited. Track referrals declined on these grounds and the prior treatment involved.

limited.t: Candidates must have an ECOG performance status of 0–1.
limited.why: Local convention. The protocol cites no source for this limit, and it is not among the OPTN Policy 9.5.A requirements the protocol lists. No data comparing pathway or transplant outcomes by performance status are cited. Track candidates excluded on performance status alone and changes in performance status during neoadjuvant therapy.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §1 Patient Selection Criteria (Inclusion Criteria)

limited.t: While listed, cross-sectional imaging and CA 19-9 are repeated every 3 months; tumor progression, new lesions, extrahepatic disease or nodal metastases lead to delisting.
limited.why: Guideline-based interval. The 3-month imaging interval cites the AASLD/AST candidate-evaluation guideline and the CA 19-9 interval is uncited; the protocol cites no study comparing surveillance intervals. OPTN separately requires imaging within 30 days before each extension request. Track metastases first found at operative staging or on the explant despite negative interval imaging, and CA 19-9 rises that led to action.

limited.t: Piggyback caval reconstruction is the institutional default where anatomy permits; the need for caval or portal resection and reconstruction is decided intraoperatively.
limited.why: Local convention. The protocol cites no comparative evidence for the default and states that no single technique is protocol-mandated. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation can cause retrohepatic caval and portal changes that require caval replacement or other vascular reconstruction, and living-donor recipients often need portal reconstruction. Track the technique used, vascular reconstructions and caval or portal complications.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §6 Liver Transplantation

limited.t: Before transplant, transplant surgery and radiation oncology review the actual radiation dose map; after transplant, Doppler ultrasound surveillance is used because of radiation-related vascular risk.
limited.why: Expert opinion. Both rules cite a Mayo expert narrative review (Tan 2020) that reports late arterial and portal complications but has no randomized comparison of reconstruction, anticoagulation or surveillance schedules; the protocol sets no Doppler interval. The high-risk protocol (§3.1) adds a 49-recipient observational comparison: major vascular complications 11/27 after chemoradiotherapy versus 3/22 without. Track hepatic artery and portal events, graft loss and retransplantation.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §6 Liver Transplantation and §9 Post-Transplant Surveillance

limited.t: Induction is a steroid bolus in the anhepatic phase; each patient has one documented maintenance strategy: tacrolimus with stepwise minimization, or mTOR-inhibitor conversion with reduced-dose tacrolimus.
limited.why: Extrapolated and observational. The induction citation is a Houston prospective case series in intrahepatic CCA (Lunsford 2018), not pCCA. The protocol states that no pCCA-specific maintenance regimen has proved to reduce recurrence; in the cited Houston cohort (Semaan 2025) the mTOR survival association was not confirmed when exposure was modeled as time-dependent. Everolimus is not started before day 30 (US label). Track strategy, rejection, renal function and recurrence.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §7 Post-Transplant Immunosuppression

limited.t: No routine adjuvant chemotherapy after a complete pathologic response; with residual tumor on the explant, capecitabine or gemcitabine-based therapy is considered only case by case or within a protocol.
limited.why: Extrapolated. The protocol states that the evidence comes from resection studies and that post-transplant benefit and tolerability are unproven; the cited source is a Houston intrahepatic CCA case series. Residual viable tumor is associated with recurrence but does not predict an individual outcome and does not by itself establish benefit from adjuvant therapy. Track adjuvant use by explant category, tolerance and recurrence.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §8 Post-Transplant Adjuvant Therapy and §10 Expected Outcomes; decision 'Surveil after transplant'

limited.t: After transplant: abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI every 6 months for 3 years, then yearly to year 5; chest imaging every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly; CA 19-9 every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months.
limited.why: Proposed local schedule. The imaging interval is the one observed in a small incidental biliary-cancer series (Heinrich 2026), not a comparative trial; NCCN describes post-resection surveillance and does not validate this transplant calendar; the CA 19-9 interval is uncited. The high-risk protocol instead proposes imaging with CA 19-9 every 3 months for 2 years. Record the adopted schedule in the decision log; track how recurrences are detected.

standard: Report local cumulative dropout from protocol entry and time-specific dropout with the clock explicitly defined; do not equate cumulative attrition with a three-month rate.
highrisk: Register every referred or screened candidate in the institutionally approved system, not only recipients. Record acceptance or rejection, treatment entry, response, listing, exception decision, conversion to resection or ablation, progression, toxicity, decompensation, death, patient withdrawal and access-related loss.

Report overall survival from the prespecified entry point and separately from listing and transplantation. Keep recurrence-free survival, recurrence incidence, graft survival and survival after recurrence distinct, with definitions, confidence intervals, numbers at risk and follow-up completeness. Do not call recipient-only survival an intention-to-treat outcome.

Capture 90-day recipient morbidity and mortality, biopsy-defined rejection, infection, arterial and biliary complications, graft loss, retransplantation and total grafts used. Record recurrence site, salvage treatment, time off systemic therapy, functional recovery and quality of life, not survival alone.

Before a transplanting study opens, biostatistics and the independent safety board must approve indication-specific monitoring, evaluable denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria. ALLOC-B4 now proposes explicit initial-cohort review triggers for ratification; they are not validated efficacy/futility boundaries. No universal cross-cancer five-year survival cutoff is adopted.

Use a contemporary comparator with the same eligibility and time zero. Account for the interval needed to survive to transplantation, crossover, competing risks and overlapping study cohorts. A nonsignificant difference is not proof of equivalence.

The cited small-tumor transplant cohorts are incidental tumors in cirrhotic explants (for example De Martin 2020); no transplant outcome data for noncirrhotic small iCCA are cited. Track noncirrhotic referrals and how they were handled.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2.1 Inclusion Criteria; decision 'Check clinical selection criteria'

limited.t: Candidates need ECOG 0–1; there is no upper age limit, but those over 70 need enhanced physiologic assessment and explicit selection-committee sign-off.
limited.why: Local rules. The protocol cites no source for ECOG 0–1. OPTN sets no age limit; the 70-year trigger and the assessment bundle (frailty, sarcopenia, cardiopulmonary, geriatric or anesthesia review) are institutional, and age alone may not be grounds to decline. The age rule cites a non-transplant eligibility cohort (Schleimer 2026); no transplant outcomes by age or performance status are cited. Track committee decisions and outcomes for these candidates.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2.1 Inclusion Criteria

limited.t: Poorly differentiated histology is a relative contraindication.
limited.why: Guideline-based (AASLD PSC/CCA guidance). The supporting cohort data are small and retrospective: in De Martin 2020, incidental tumors in cirrhosis, tumor grade carried a hazard ratio of 3.74. A core biopsy cannot guarantee the grade of the whole tumor, and the protocol does not define how the relative contraindication is weighed. Track biopsy versus explant grade and recurrence by grade.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2.2 Exclusion Criteria

limited.t: Macrovascular invasion excludes the candidate.
limited.why: Local exclusion. It is not among the NLRB criteria the protocol lists, and the cited source (Schleimer 2026) is a non-transplant eligibility cohort; the Houston advanced-iCCA series also excluded major vascular encasement. No transplant outcome comparison by vascular invasion is cited. The open high-risk review would allow encasement without tumor thrombus in the advanced study. Track vascular findings on the explant.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2.2 Exclusion Criteria

related.label: iCCA-B1 · Advanced disease: tumor distribution and grade

limited.t: Prior liver resection does not by itself exclude a candidate; recurrent or other outside-guidance presentations need explicit multidisciplinary and individual allocation review.
limited.why: Clinical reasoning. NLRB guidance does not list prior resection as an exclusion. The only transplant experience after resection that the protocol cites is a single-center advanced-iCCA series in which four previously resected patients were listed and three transplanted (McMillan 2022); that research cohort does not establish eligibility for the standard route. Track previously resected candidates, selection decisions and recurrence.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §2.2 Exclusion Criteria

limited.t: If checkpoint-inhibitor therapy is used, a washout of at least 90 days precedes transplant; afterwards, liver tests are checked twice weekly for 4 weeks, then weekly to week 12, with biopsy for unexplained rises.
limited.why: Protocol convention. The protocol calls the 90-day washout a convention, not a validated threshold: no interval has been shown to eliminate rejection, and rejection has been reported after longer intervals. Evidence is retrospective and largely HCC-derived (Moeckli 2025, VITALITY). The monitoring schedule is a local operational rule; pooled retrospective data (8 studies, n = 229) show 19% rejection with no reliable onset time. Track washout, rejection and graft loss.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §4.1 Systemic Therapy and §7.2 Maintenance; decision 'Plan pretransplant treatment'

related.label: Which control strategy and ICI safety rules will be used?

limited.t: For living donation, recipient staging and technical clearance are completed before irreversible donor surgery, with an explicit abort plan for occult nodes, peritoneal disease or unresectability.
limited.why: Operational safety proposal. The protocol labels this a safety workflow, not proof that negative staging prevents recurrence. The cited UPMC series (Sethi 2026) staged recipients before donor surgery and aborted 7 of 31 explorations, but it included only seven iCCA recipients. Track aborted donor and recipient operations and occult disease found at staging.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §6.1 Staging Laparotomy

related.label: iCCA-B3 · Living-donor transplantation: study readiness

limited.t: At transplant, perihepatic lymph nodes are sampled for frozen section; extrahepatic or extrabiliary spread on frozen section aborts the transplant and the organ is reallocated.
limited.why: Single-center protocol. The rule follows the Houston prospective case series (Lunsford 2018), in which six patients were transplanted. The protocol gives no data on frozen-section accuracy, and it notes that negative EUS sampling does not exclude all nodal disease. Track agreement between frozen-section and final pathology, and aborted transplants.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §6.1 Staging Laparotomy

limited.t: No routine adjuvant therapy after a complete pathologic response; with residual viable tumor, chemotherapy is considered only case by case or within a prospective protocol.
limited.why: Extrapolated. The protocol states that no post-transplant adjuvant standard exists and that benefit and tolerability in immunosuppressed recipients are unproven; the cited source is a single-center case series (Lunsford 2018). Track adjuvant use, tolerance and recurrence by explant response.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §8 Adjuvant Therapy Post-Transplant; decision 'Transplant and follow-up'

limited.t: After transplant, chest CT plus abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI every 3 months in years 1–2 and every 6 months in years 3–5, with CA 19-9 and CEA at each visit, then annual follow-up as indicated.
limited.why: Institutional proposal. The protocol states this is not the schedule of the cited incidental biliary-cancer series (Heinrich 2026), which imaged every 6 months for 3 years and then annually; selected transplant data do not define an optimal interval. The group is to approve modality, interval, contrast adaptations and escalation triggers and record the rationale. Track how recurrences are detected.
limited.locator: Standard pathway document §9.1 Oncologic Surveillance; decision 'Transplant and follow-up'

related.label: What post-transplant recurrence surveillance will the program adopt?

limited.t: After confirmed recurrence, transplant hepatology, surgery and oncology discuss individualized immunosuppression minimization.
limited.why: Single-center retrospective association. In the cited cohort (Gül-Klein 2022: 67 recipients with mixed CCA subtypes, 1988–2022), restrictive immunosuppression was associated with longer survival after recurrence, but selection and confounding limit causal inference, and mTOR use showed no independent association. The protocol supports consideration, not automatic withdrawal or routine mTOR substitution. Track rejection and survival after minimization.

standard: Every removal and every reactivation is recorded with its category and the supporting evidence.
highrisk: Register every referred or screened candidate in the institutionally approved system, not only recipients. Record acceptance or rejection, treatment entry, response, listing, exception decision, conversion to resection or ablation, progression, toxicity, decompensation, death, patient withdrawal and access-related loss.

Report overall survival from the prespecified entry point and separately from listing and transplantation. Keep recurrence-free survival, recurrence incidence, graft survival and survival after recurrence distinct, with definitions, confidence intervals, numbers at risk and follow-up completeness. Do not call recipient-only survival an intention-to-treat outcome.

Capture 90-day recipient morbidity and mortality, biopsy-defined rejection, infection, arterial and biliary complications, graft loss, retransplantation and total grafts used. Record recurrence site, salvage treatment, time off systemic therapy, functional recovery and quality of life, not survival alone.

Before a transplanting study opens, biostatistics and the independent safety board must approve indication-specific monitoring, evaluable denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria. ALLOC-B4 now proposes explicit initial-cohort review triggers for ratification; they are not validated efficacy/futility boundaries. No universal cross-cancer five-year survival cutoff is adopted.

Use a contemporary comparator with the same eligibility and time zero. Account for the interval needed to survive to transplantation, crossover, competing risks and overlapping study cohorts. A nonsignificant difference is not proof of equivalence.

summary.lead: Liver transplant + chemotherapy vs chemotherapy alone
summary.text: Five-year ITT OS 56.6% vs 12.6%, HR 0.37 (95% CI 0.21–0.65); 26 of 36 per-protocol recipients recurred

appraisal.note: Trial selection and outcomes support a selected permanently unresectable population; trial eligibility is not interchangeable with NLRB guidance.
appraisal.scope: Multicentre open-label randomized trial, 20 European centres, 157 screened and 94 randomized (47 LT-plus-chemotherapy, 47 chemotherapy); 63 screened excluded, including 13 with equivocal unresectability and 36 with progression.
appraisal.results: Primary time origin was randomization. Median follow-up 59.3 months. Five-year ITT OS was 56.6% versus 12.6% (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21–0.65); per-protocol OS 73.3% versus 9.3%. Of 47 assigned LT, 38 received LT and 36 were per-protocol; nine had progression-related exclusion/dropout. The control arm included seven subsequent resections and two LT crossovers. Safety population comprised 40 grafted patients. Among 36 per-protocol LT recipients, 26 recurred; 19/26 received chemotherapy and 12/26 local curative-intent treatment. Median per-protocol PFS was 17.4 versus 6.4 months, and secondary PFS after salvage was 35.4 months in the LT arm. Three of 36 per-protocol recipients required retransplantation (primary nonfunction, donor gallbladder cancer, caval obstruction/large-for-size); one postoperative death was reported. Serious adverse events occurred in 32/40 safety LT recipients. Median wait to LT was 50.5 days, which limits transfer to longer-wait systems.
appraisal.limitations: Strong evidence for the selected trial population, not for BRAF-mutant, ECOG 2, active extrahepatic, truly NED, resectable or broadly expanded disease. PP survival conditions on reaching treatment and must not replace ITT. The Results recurrence denominator is 26/36; Figure 3 caption says 28 recurrences, consistent with a broader all-grafted report, so do not mix these denominators. QoL collection had only 55/74 per-protocol baseline questionnaires and is descriptive, not proof of a large QoL gain. Priority allocation and rapid access were part of the treatment strategy.

appraisal.scope: Single-centre retrospective HAIP cohort: 1,110 patients treated in 2006–2016, 483 initially unresectable after exclusions; 83 met modified transplant criteria, but only 23 were pretreated, chemotherapy-controlled transplant-like candidates.
appraisal.results: Time zero was HAIP placement, not a common LT-versus-HAIP eligibility date. In the 23 selected pretreated patients, 18/23 (78%) converted to resection; only 10/18 were R0, and 17/18 recurred, with salvage treatment in 15. Median follow-up was 97.7 months; median OS 61 months (95% CI 36–92), five-year OS 53% (36–79), PFS 13 months (9.6–22), hepatic PFS 16 months (11–61). Median treatment comprised five HAIP cycles and nine systemic cycles. Biliary sclerosis requiring stents occurred in 3/23 (13%); one pump-arterial dissection required revision.

The high conversion rate is clinically important counterevidence to declaring unresectability before specialist conversion review. It does not make HAIP compulsory or establish that its toxicities are an indication to create for LT.

Two-year non-recurrence is not pathology; evaluability selection and noncentral imaging review are limitations. Neither disappearance equals cure nor uncertain viability requires removal/LT. The cited 2014 London consensus, based on low-quality observational evidence, lists severe carcinoid heart disease, not every echocardiographic abnormality, as a contraindication; NCCN ties valve replacement to significant or symptomatic disease. NCCN 2026 states that prophylactic octreotide is probably ineffective at preventing intraoperative crisis, yet still allows selective prophylactic use while questioning routine use; no transplant-specific study is cited. limited.t: Immunosuppression follows the institutional LT protocol (intraoperative methylprednisolone, tacrolimus-based maintenance); everolimus is optional, not before day 30, and not given as cancer prophylaxis.
limited.why: Extrapolated from general LT practice. AASLD/AST guidance supports individualised tacrolimus-based therapy, and its mTOR recommendation is limited to HCC within Milan; the SiLVER HCC trial's primary endpoint was negative. No NET-specific regimen has been shown to reduce recurrence, and the day-30 everolimus limit is a label safety floor. Track rejection, renal function and recurrence by regimen.

limited.t: Post-transplant oncologic surveillance is every 3 months to month 24 and every 6 months in years 3–5, with SSTR-PET only when indicated and individualised follow-up with no fixed stopping point.

NCCN surveillance schedules are for non-transplant patients, and the protocol states that no validated post-transplant calendar exists and that any intensified local calendar is institutional consensus. Recurrence has been documented up to 204 months after transplant in the Milan series, which supports long follow-up but not a specific interval. limited.t: Every post-transplant recurrence goes to tumour board, and complete salvage resection is considered for technically resectable, biologically favourable recurrence.
limited.why: Single-centre series. In the 32-patient Milan recurrence cohort, surgery versus other treatment was associated with 5-year post-recurrence survival of 90.9% versus 64.5% (P=.062), an unadjusted, non-significant comparison confounded by selection and resectability. Recurrence within 24 months is a risk marker, not a validated bar to salvage. Track salvage procedures, complications and survival after recurrence.

limited.t: Post-transplant PRRT is investigational: considered case by case only for SSTR-positive recurrence, after joint transplant-oncology, nuclear-medicine, hepatology and pharmacy review, preferably in a protocol.

Track marrow, renal and graft toxicity and response.

highrisk: Register every referred or screened candidate in the institutionally approved system, not only recipients. Record acceptance or rejection, treatment entry, response, listing, exception decision, conversion to resection or ablation, progression, toxicity, decompensation, death, patient withdrawal and access-related loss.

Report overall survival from the prespecified entry point and separately from listing and transplantation. Keep recurrence-free survival, recurrence incidence, graft survival and survival after recurrence distinct, with definitions, confidence intervals, numbers at risk and follow-up completeness. Do not call recipient-only survival an intention-to-treat outcome.

Capture 90-day recipient morbidity and mortality, biopsy-defined rejection, infection, arterial and biliary complications, graft loss, retransplantation and total grafts used. Record recurrence site, salvage treatment, time off systemic therapy, functional recovery and quality of life, not survival alone.

Before a transplanting study opens, biostatistics and the independent safety board must approve indication-specific monitoring, evaluable denominators, pause authority and reopening criteria. ALLOC-B4 now proposes explicit initial-cohort review triggers for ratification; they are not validated efficacy/futility boundaries. No universal cross-cancer five-year survival cutoff is adopted.

Use a contemporary comparator with the same eligibility and time zero. Account for the interval needed to survive to transplantation, crossover, competing risks and overlapping study cohorts. A nonsignificant difference is not proof of equivalence.

limited.t: Biopsy is reserved for atypical imaging, suspected malignant transformation, or when molecular subtype will change management, and targets the dominant or most suspicious lesion.
limited.why: Guideline-consistent, with limited data for lesion choice. ACG notes that MRI cannot reliably identify β-catenin activation or separate HCA from well-differentiated HCC. Sampling the dominant lesion rests on one molecular cohort (Nault 2017): subtype differed between tumors in 21 of 73 patients with several sampled lesions, and the exon 3 mutation was in the largest tumor in 8 of 9 relevant cases. Track subtype by lesion sampled and biopsy-explant concordance.

limited.t: With Abernethy malformation, shunt closure or another vascular intervention is assessed before transplantation.
limited.why: Expert opinion. The protocol cites no source for this sequence and no data comparing shunt closure with transplantation. In the cited European series (Chiche 2016), seven of 49 recipients had vascular abnormalities, which added technical complexity. Track shunt-closure attempts, adenoma response and later need for transplantation.

limited.t: While listed, multiphasic MRI or CT is repeated every 3 months, aligned with the 90-day exception-extension cycle, and sooner for growth, hemorrhage or suspected transformation.
limited.why: Local convention. The interval follows the administrative 90-day extension cycle rather than adenoma natural-history data, and the protocol cites no study of waiting-list imaging intervals. In the cited UNOS analysis, 18 of 199 listed patients died or became too sick for transplant, a crude figure without lesion detail. Track waiting-list hemorrhage, rupture, malignant transformation and dropout.

limited.t: After transplant, no routine tumor imaging if the explant shows no malignancy; with occult or known malignant transformation, chest and abdominal imaging every 3–6 months for 2 years, then every 6 months to year 5.
limited.why: Clinical reasoning and extrapolation from HCC follow-up. The protocol cites no source for either schedule. In the cited European series (Chiche 2016), three HCC recurrences occurred among 49 recipients, all fatal, so explant pathology decides which schedule applies. Track explant malignancy, adherence to the assigned schedule and recurrence.

summary.lead: Multicentre molecular cohort · 533 adenomas in 411 patients
summary.text: Symptomatic bleeding 14%, HCC 3%; size did not predict symptomatic bleeding (P=0.29) or malignancy (P=0.053); CTNNB1 exon 3 OR 9.3 for borderline/HCC

appraisal.note: Molecular risk stratification informs clinical judgment. Any local restriction to a particular β-catenin exon must be distinguished from the NLRB criteria for MELD-exception review.
appraisal.scope: Molecular study: 533 adenomas from 411 patients across 28 centers.
appraisal.results: Symptomatic bleeding in 14% of patients; 3% developed HCC. Strong exon-3 CTNNB1 activation tracks malignant risk; exon-7/8 activation is biologically different; sonic-hedgehog subtype associates with bleeding.
appraisal.limitations: Observed prevalence is not individual lifetime risk. Molecular risk supports definitive-treatment assessment, not automatic LT or equivalence of all β-catenin variants.
